subject: Divergent Transitions when Parameterizing Beta Distro in terms of Mean and Variance

messages.author: 596a0b6cc13c8414
messages.subject: Divergent Transitions when Parameterizing Beta Distro in terms of Mean and Variance
parts:
I'm a not very experienced stan user trying to fit a model in rstan that involves a beta distribution parameterized by its mean and variance (i.e. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution#Mean_and_variance).  Here's the model (although this assumes one treatment level w, I want to analyze several treatment levels simultaneously).

The estimates stan provides seem reasonably close to the simulated data, however I'm getting a lot of divergent transitions. I'm trying now to figure out how to address this problem, if indeed it is really a problem I should be concerned about.

With the default settings I typically get 500+ divergent transitions.  The divergent transitions typically have to do with the parameters of the beta distribution being less than 0. Bumping up the adapt_delta to 0.999 reduces the typical number to around 50. Is this an acceptable number?

One thing to note is that my stan code does not explicitly account for the constraint that sigma2 < mu(1-mu).  The reason I didn't include this is that I wasn't sure about including parameters of the model as constraints.  I looked in the documentation and saw that you can do this, however the examples presented there involve scalar bounds and I want to treat mu and sigma2 as arrays (so as to analyze simultaneously multiple treatment levels).  A line like real<lower=0,upper=mu*(1-mu)> sigma2[K];  doesn't seem valid.

Below is the code I'm using (any other tips appreciated!). 

data {
    int<lower=0> K; //number of levels
    real<lower=0,upper=1> w[K]; //treatment level 
    int y[K]; //number of responses at each treatment level
    int N[K]; //number assigned to each level
}
parameters {
    real beta0; 
    real beta1;
    real<lower=0> gamma;
    real<lower=0,upper=1> pi[K]; //propensity to respond
}
transformed parameters{
    real<lower=0,upper=1> mu[K];
    real<lower=0> sigma2[K];  //variance
    real<lower=0> alpha[K];
    real<lower=0> beta[K];
    for (j in 1:K)
        mu[j] <- inv_logit(beta0 + beta1*w[j]); //expected response rate
    for (j in 1:K)
    sigma2[j] <- gamma*w[j]*(1-w[j]); //variance in response at level
    for (j in 1:K)
        alpha[j] <- (mu[j]^2 *(1-mu[j]^2))/sigma2[j] - mu[j]; 
    for (j in 1:K)
        beta[j] <- (mu[j] - 1)*(1 + (mu[j]*(mu[j]-1))/sigma2[j]); #
}
model {
    for (j in 1:K)
        pi[j] ~ beta(alpha[j],beta[j]);
    for (j in 1:K)
        y[j] ~ binomial(N[j],pi[j]);
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent Transitions when Parameterizing Beta Distro in terms of Mean and Variance
parts:
You need the constraints to make sure alpha
and beta are positive.

I'd suggest using an alternative parameterization that
we suggest in the manual and Andrew uses in Bayesian
Data Analysis, where you use


vector<lower=0>[K] kappa;
vector<lower=0, upper=1>[K] theta;

alpha[i] <- k[i] * theta[i];
beta[i] <- k[i] * (1 - theta[i]);

theta is the mean parameterization, but kappa is the prior
count (plus 2), and thus acts like a precision parameter.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Divergent Transitions when Parameterizing Beta Distro in terms of Mean and Variance
parts:
If you change it from 0.1, you also have to change the
first parameter of the Pareto to match. And it has to
be a value > 0. You can use something other than the Pareto
as a prior --- I was just using it to match Gelman et al.'s
Bayesian Data Analysis, chapter 5. But Andrew's not at all
wedded to that prior.

- Bob
